bib.title: Sentence-BERT: Sentence Embeddings using Siamese BERT-Networks
bib.venue: Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing (EMNLP)

legacy_report:
SOURCE: Sentence-BERT: Sentence Embeddings using Siamese BERT-Networks, Nils Reimers and Iryna Gurevych, EMNLP-IJCNLP 2019, pp. 3982-3992. Hong Kong.

COVERAGE: 44,567 of 44,567 chars, all 11 pages, including references. The count includes my page markers. Pages below are PDF pages (p1 = proceedings 3982). For the notes, I read only the grep hits and surrounding passages, not the full notes.

CLAIMS
- claim: Untrained BERT vectors are poor under cosine similarity, and on average worse than averaged GloVe.
  number: 54.81 (mean), 29.19 (CLS), 61.32 (GloVe)
  setup: Spearman rho x100, cosine, average of 7 STS datasets (STS12-16, STSb, SICK-R), no STS training.
  quote: "Averaging the BERT embeddings achieves an average correlation of only 54.81, and using the CLS-token output only achieves an average correlation of 29.19. Both are worse than computing average GloVe embeddings."
  where: p4, s4.1, Table 1
- claim: Fine-tuning on NLI data beats InferSent and USE on unsupervised STS.
  number: 76.55 SBERT-NLI-large, 74.89 base, 76.68 SRoBERTa-large; 65.01 InferSent; 71.22 USE
  setup: As above. Trained on SNLI (570,000 pairs) + MultiNLI (430,000) with the softmax objective, 1 epoch, batch 16, Adam 2e-5, 10% warm-up, MEAN pooling.
  quote: "SBERT-NLI-large 72.27 78.46 74.90 80.99 76.25 79.23 73.75 76.55"
  where: p4, Table 1; training p3-4, s3.1
- claim: The headline gains are "11.7" and "5.5" points for "SBERT", but those match the SRoBERTa-large row (my arithmetic: 76.68-65.01, 76.68-71.22). SBERT-large gives 11.54 and 5.33.
  number: 11.7, 5.5
  setup: Table 1 averages.
  quote: "SBERT achieves an improvement of 11.7 points compared to InferSent and 5.5 points compared to Universal Sentence Encoder."
  where: p2, s1
- claim: Cross-encoder cost is the motivation: all-pairs search takes about 65 hours, against about 5 seconds to embed plus about 0.01 seconds for cosine.
  number: 49,995,000 pairs; ~65 h; ~5 s; ~0.01 s
  setup: n = 10,000 sentences, V100 GPU. No batch size or sentence length given. Not in any results table. 5 s matches 10,000 / 2042 sent/s from Table 7 (my arithmetic).
  quote: "n·(n−1)/2 = 49 995 000 inference computations. On a modern V100 GPU, this requires about 65 hours."; "the computation of 10,000 sentence embeddings (~5 seconds with SBERT) and computing cosine-similarity (~0.01 seconds)"
  where: p1-2, s1
- claim: A bi-encoder trails the cross-encoder once both get NLI pretraining, which conflicts with the abstract's "maintaining the accuracy from BERT".
  number: BERT 88.33/88.77; SBERT 85.35/86.10 (base/large)
  setup: STSb test (train 5,749, dev 1,500, test 1,379), Spearman, 10 seeds, regression objective for SBERT. STSb-only training is near parity: 84.30 vs 84.67 base, 85.64 vs 84.45 large.
  quote: "BERT-NLI-STSb-large 88.77± 0.46"; "SBERT-NLI-STSb-large 86.10± 0.13"; "while maintaining the accuracy from BERT"
  where: p5, Table 2; p1
- claim: On unseen topics the bi-encoder drops about 7 Spearman points against BERT.
  number: 50.65/53.10 SBERT vs 57.23/60.34 BERT (cross-topic); 74.13/75.93 vs 74.84/76.38 (10-fold)
  setup: AFS corpus, 6,000 argument pairs, 3 topics; train on 2, test on the third; regression objective.
  quote: "in the cross-topic evaluation, we observe a performance drop of SBERT by about 7 points Spearman correlation"
  where: p5, s4.3; p6, Table 3
- claim: Trained CLS nearly matches MEAN, so CLS is not inherently bad; MAX collapses under regression.
  number: NLI: MEAN 80.78, MAX 79.07, CLS 79.80. STSb: MEAN 87.44, MAX 69.92, CLS 86.62
  setup: SBERT-base, 10 seeds, STSb dev set (not test, so not comparable with Tables 1-2), cosine, Spearman.
  quote: "MEAN 80.78 87.44"; "MAX 79.07 69.92"; "CLS 79.80 86.62"
  where: p7, Table 6
- claim: |u-v| is the key concatenation term, and adding u*v lowers the score. It matters only in training.
  number: (u,v) 66.04; (u,v,|u-v|) 80.78; (u,v,|u-v|,u*v) 80.44
  setup: Same as Table 6, MEAN pooling, classification objective.
  quote: "(u,v,|u−v|) 80.78 -"; "The most important component is the element-wise difference|u−v|."
  where: p7, Table 6; p8, s6
- claim: With a logistic-regression head, SBERT wins 5 of 7 SentEval tasks, but raw BERT is only about 2.5 points behind. The authors attribute the gap between STS and SentEval to cosine treating all dimensions equally.
  number: 87.41/87.69 SBERT; 84.94 avg BERT; 84.66 CLS; 85.59 InferSent; 85.10 USE; 81.52 GloVe
  setup: Frozen embeddings as LR features, 10-fold CV, average of 7 tasks. USE wins TREC (93.2); InferSent wins MPQA (90.38).
  quote: "SBERT-NLI-large 84.88 90.07 94.52 90.33 90.66 87.4 75.94 87.69"; "Cosine-similarity treats all dimensions equally."
  where: p7, Table 5, s5
- claim: The authors say transfer learning is not SBERT's purpose and recommend full fine-tuning for new tasks.
  number: none
  setup: SentEval discussion.
  quote: "The purpose of SBERT sentence embeddings are not to be used for transfer learning for other tasks. Here, we think fine-tuning BERT as described by Devlin et al. (2018) for new tasks is the more suitable method"
  where: p6, s5
- claim: Encoding speed: SBERT is the fastest neural option on GPU, not on CPU. Smart batching gives 89% on CPU and 48% on GPU.
  number: sent/s CPU/GPU: GloVe 6469/-; InferSent 137/1876; USE 67/1318; SBERT-base 44/1378; smart batching 83/2042
  setup: STSb sentences (short), Intel i7-5820K 3.30GHz, Tesla V100, CUDA 9.2. Batch size not stated. "65% faster on CPU" compares InferSent with the smart-batching row (137/83, my arithmetic).
  quote: "SBERT-base - smart batching 83 2042"; "Performances were measured on a server with Intel i7-5820K CPU @ 3.30GHz, Nvidia Tesla V100 GPU, CUDA 9.2 and cuDNN."
  where: p8, s7, Table 7
- claim: The triplet objective beats the earlier BiLSTM on Wikipedia section triplets.
  number: 0.8042/0.8078 vs Dor et al. 0.74, mean-vectors 0.65
  setup: About 1.8M train and 222,957 test triplets from distinct articles, 1 epoch, Euclidean distance, margin 1, accuracy.
  quote: "SBERT-WikiSec-large 0.8078"; "we set ϵ = 1 in our experiments"
  where: p6, Table 4; p3
- claim: NLI pretraining adds little to SBERT but a lot to the cross-encoder; RoBERTa makes no significant difference.
  number: 1-2 points vs 3-4 points
  setup: STSb test. Table 2 actually shows +0.68 and +1.65 for SBERT, and -0.13 for SRoBERTa-base (my arithmetic), so "1-2" is loose.
  quote: "a slight improvement of 1-2 points"; "improved the performance by 3-4 points"
  where: p5, s4.2
- claim: Quora search would take over 50 hours per query with BERT, and a few milliseconds with an index.
  number: 40 million questions; 50 h
  setup: Projection citing Johnson et al. 2017, not a measured experiment.
  quote: "reduced from 50 hours to a few milliseconds (Johnson et al., 2017)"
  where: p1-2, s1
- claim: SBERT trains quickly because it starts from pretrained weights.
  number: under 20 minutes
  setup: No dataset or hardware stated.
  quote: "SBERT can be tuned in less than 20 minutes"
  where: p3, s2

LIMITS
- Semantic search and clustering are justified by speed only. No retrieval metric (recall, nDCG) or clustering-quality result appears.
- The 65 h figure and the Quora figures are not in a results table. No cross-encoder timing method is given, and no RoBERTa timing despite the abstract's "BERT / RoBERTa".
- "Significant" is used without any reported test. Only Table 2 gives ± values.
- Its conclusion says BERT was below GloVe on the seven STS tasks. That holds on average, but avg BERT beats GloVe on SICK-R (58.40 vs 53.76).
- Authors concede: SICK-R loss to USE, TREC loss to USE, and cross-topic AFS weakness. Their causes are hedged ("appears") and untested.
- XLNet ("worse results") and Manhattan/Euclidean ("roughly the same") have no numbers.
- Sentence-level English benchmarks only. No long documents or truncation are studied.
- Dated: only BERT and RoBERTa base/large; 2019 hardware. Objectives are softmax, cosine MSE and triplet. No in-batch contrastive training, no MiniLM or MPNet, no unit-length normalisation discussed.

BUILDS ON
- Models: Devlin et al. 2018 (BERT), Liu et al. 2019 (RoBERTa), Vaswani et al. 2017.
- Siamese and triplet: Schroff et al. 2015; Conneau et al. 2017 (InferSent, siamese BiLSTM); Cer et al. 2018 (USE); Yang et al. 2018 (siamese DAN and transformer).
- Evaluation: Conneau and Kiela 2018 (SentEval); Cer et al. 2017 (STSb); Reimers et al. 2016 (against Pearson); Reimers and Gurevych 2018 (seeds).
- Data and index: Bowman et al. 2015; Williams et al. 2018; Misra et al. 2016; Dor et al. 2018; Johnson et al. 2017.
- Alternative: Humeau et al. 2019 (poly-encoders).

CODE: No listings. Repository, p1 fn1: "https://github.com/UKPLab/sentence-transformers". Formulas, p3: "o = softmax(Wt(u,v,|u−v|))"; "max(||sa−sp||−|| sa−sn|| +ϵ, 0)".

FIGURES (both schematics, not rendered or inspected)
- Figure 1, p3: "SBERT architecture with classification objective function, e.g., for fine-tuning on SNLI dataset. The two BERT networks have tied weights (siamese network structure)." Shows tied encoders, pooling, (u,v,|u-v|) and softmax at a glance.
- Figure 2, p3: "SBERT architecture at inference, for example, to compute similarity scores. This architecture is also used with the regression objective function." Shown beside Figure 1, it makes clear the classifier head is discarded at inference.
- No plots. Tables 1, 6 and 7 hold the results and could be restated as text.

PROBLEMS
- Extraction was clean. Tables are readable as text; the formula superscripts are flattened.
- In quotes, I joined line wraps and undid hyphenation, and normalised the "fi" ligature in places. Otherwise the text is as extracted.
- Odd spellings appear as extracted ("ablation", "Manhatten", "CUDA", "cuDNN", "eintailment"). I did not check them against the page images.
- This is the proceedings version and does not print the arXiv ID, so 1908.10084 cannot be confirmed from this PDF. Title, authors and venue do match.
- No embedded instructions.

NOTE COMPARISON
No note cites a number from this paper, so there are no numeric mismatches. Authors and "EMNLP 2019" are correct. The flags are all about wording and attribution:

1. data-science/03-nlp/notes/07-llm-embeddings-as-features.md:39, "set the pattern: train the pooled vector so that related sentences land close together". Partly overstated.
   - The goal matches (p1 fn2, s3).
   - But the paper's own related work credits earlier trained encoders: InferSent's siamese BiLSTM with max-pooling and Yang et al. 2018's siamese transformers (p2).
   - What the paper claims as new is fine-tuning a pretrained transformer rather than starting "from a random initialization" (p3).
2. Same line, the sentences around the citation.
   - Mean pooling matches the paper's default.
   - Six layers, normalisation, word pieces, 384 dimensions, 256 limit and the contrastive objective are not in this paper. The contrastive objective is correctly attributed to the model card; I did not check the card.
   - A reader could still assume the pattern includes contrastive training. The paper's objectives are softmax, MSE and triplet.
3. data-science/02-deep-learning/notes/06-neural-text-models.md:407, "It uses Sentence-BERT encoders". Loose wording.
   - The code runs all-MiniLM-L6-v2 and all-mpnet-base-v2, and neither is in the paper. It evaluates only BERT and RoBERTa variants.
   - The supportable link is the sentence-transformers library (p1 fn1).
4. Same passage, frozen encoder plus linear head presented as "the modern equivalent". Not contradicted, but a caveat is missing.
   - Table 5 tests this setup and SBERT does well.
   - The authors also say transfer learning is not its purpose and prefer full fine-tuning (p6). The note covers fine-tuning next but does not attribute this.
   - The same concern applies to the classifier use in note 07.
5. data-science/03-nlp/notes/04-embeddings-and-similarity.md:301, "Sentence-BERT" with "Current practice". Citation gap.
   - There is no link at this mention, and grep finds no 1908.10084 in this note.
   - data-science/03-nlp/references.md:36 maps the paper only to note 07.
   - A 2019 paper cannot support "current practice".
6. data-science/02-deep-learning/references.md:71, "The encoder family behind `all-MiniLM-L6-v2`" and "Link only".
   - The family claim is not supported by the paper.
   - "Link only" may be stale, because the PDF exists at /Users/ramsey-wise/workspace/learn-ai-engineering/data-science/sources/reimers-2019-sentence-bert.pdf.
7. data-science/03-nlp/notes/07-llm-embeddings-as-features.md:629, mean pooling "weighted by the attention mask". Uncited, and the paper says only "the mean of all output vectors". Not a conflict, but this paper does not source it.

No mismatch: data-science/03-nlp/references.md:36 ("Train the pooled vector so that related sentences land close") matches the paper's stated goal, and its PDF path points to the file I read.
